catalog_quote: Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic; it falls on the penultimate syllable, and shifts to the right when suffixes are added (for exceptions, see below). For example, [wañú.špa] 'dying' ... wañu.či.ri.naya.ju.či.špa] 'to cause to be desiring to cause to commit suicide' ... Stress may be used paralinguistically for semantic focus. Stress is placed on the root or suffix carrying the contrastive semantic load. ... In the more innovative dialects, there are some exceptions to stress placement. For example, [šamu.nú.n] /šamu.nú.n/ 'they are coming (Npo.)' [kaŋ.gá] /kan.ká/ 'and you? (Imb.)' [kay.pi.ráh] /kay.pi.rák/ 'still here? (Imb.)' ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-phonemic) and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; as suffixes are added the stress moves rightward so that it stays penultimate in the full suffixed word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated about secondary stress (Carpenter's transcriptions mark only one stress per word). Aschmann 2020 likewise says nothing on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Paralinguistic/contrastive focus can place stress on the root or on a particular suffix; (ii) in 'more innovative dialects' certain suffixes attract final stress: Napo distributive /-nú-/, and the independent suffixes /-ka/ 'topic' and /-rak/ 'still' in interrogatives (Imbabura examples); transcription convention (p.~20) uses an acute for non-penultimate stress, e.g. interrogative wagraná 'a cow?'. Aschmann 2020 §4.1 fn.23 adds: accent may shift to the final syllable of the sentence-final word in some cases; Imbabura/Upper Napo phrase-terminator suffixes sometimes fall outside the stress domain; none of these exceptions is attributed specifically to Pichincha/Calderón.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (suffixed) phonological word; statement is for Ecuadorian Quichua generally, with the phonology chapter explicitly based on the non-central dialect group that includes Pichincha (Calderón, Cayambe, Guallabamba, Quinche, Checa, Puembo, Tumbaco, Sangolquí were field sites), though Carpenter notes most chapter data come from Imbabura, Cañar, Loja and Napo. Corroborated for 'Pichincha / Salcedo (= Calderón) Quichua' among all Ecuadorian varieties by Aschmann 2020 §4.1 p.20 ('falling in almost all cases on the penultimate syllable') and pp.39-40 ('Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic, and always falls on the penultimate syllable'), and historically by Grimm 1896 p.1 ('Las palabras quichuas se acentúan ordinariamente en la penúltima sílaba').
new_statements.identity_note: No source found is devoted to Calderón (Pichincha) Quichua alone. Carpenter 1982 is a pan-Ecuadorian-Quichua dissertation whose phonology chapter is explicitly based on the 'non-central' dialect group that includes Pichincha (Calderón, Cayambe and six other Pichincha field sites) alongside Imbabura (imba1240), Cañar (cana1260), Loja (loja1240), S. Chimborazo and Napo; the stress rule is stated for all of them with dialect-specific exceptions only for Imbabura and Napo. Aschmann 2020 names 'Pichincha / Salcedo Quichua, also known as Calderón Quichua' as one of the varieties covered and states the same rule for all Ecuadorian Quichua. Glottolog's cald1236 phonology reference (Kohlberger 2010) actually describes Cotopaxi (Tigua) Quichua. Grimm 1896 describes Quito-area highland Quichua generally.
